source.title: Conditional Importance in Toy Models of Superposition

record.file_problem: The supplied text includes the full post, but some mathematical notation is missing or garbled and the referenced plots are not rendered. The prose describes the main plot results.
record.tranche_reason: Tests the superposition mechanism in toy networks using conditional-importance and feature-value conditions; it uses the toy-model setup but reports results for a modified question and comparison.
record.gate_note: The post reports aggregate qualitative outcomes for three random seeds per condition, not per-seed values. Referenced results from Anthropic are background only and are not rows. The text describes phase visualizations, but the phase plots themselves are not available in the supplied text.
record.test_reason: The post uses the Toy Models of Superposition setup to ask whether conditional importance makes superposition easier than fixed importance or anti-correlated features. It measures superposition geometry: features represented in a 10-dimensional linear latent space and interference in the Gram matrix. That latent space has no activation function and so no privileged neuron basis. No neuron's polysemanticity is measured, and nothing links polysemantic neurons to superposition. So V3, which concerns why neurons are polysemantic, is not tested. The results are a related construct and are recorded under fits_no_version.
record.authors_conclusion: Correct. Features that are never important at the same time are not superposed more easily; their values must be anti-correlated. Recasting conditional importance as context-specific anti-correlated features permits more superposition and lower loss.
record.recipe_differences: Builds on the Toy Models of Superposition projection-and-recovery setup, adding conditional importance and comparing it with fixed importance and feature-value zeroing. The study uses synthetic toy networks rather than trained full-scale networks.
record.method_sensitivity: The qualitative Gram-matrix patterns vary across random initializations and synthetic data, though the author says the runs are qualitatively similar. The result also differs between conditional importance and feature values zeroed by condition, and between the original X and context-specific Z representations.

fits_no_version.finding: In a 20-to-10 linear-ReLU toy model, conditional (anti-correlated) importance yields the same superposition as fixed importance. In both, roughly 16-18 features are represented and there is within-subset interference. Anti-correlated feature values instead yield all 20 features represented with zero within-subset interference.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Superposition in toy models is increased by anti-correlated feature values, not by anti-correlated feature importance.

record.peer_reviewed: LessWrong post; peer-review status not stated
record.problems: The evidence is from a small synthetic toy setup, not trained full-scale networks. Outcomes are mainly qualitative and aggregated across three random seeds per condition; no uncertainty estimates or per-seed measurements are reported. The supplied text does not render the referenced plots and has missing or garbled mathematical notation.
record.rows_left_out: No claim-relevant outcomes omitted. The post mentions phase visualizations and loss progression, but the supplied text gives no plotted phase values; the reported phase details do not separately measure the claim.

untested.parts: Whether polysemantic neurons arise from superposition; the hidden layer has no privileged basis.
Activation function or architecture effects; other nonlinearities are proposed only as future work.

record.verdict_notes: Of the reader's choices, V3 'tests' and its 'supports' label are removed. Superposition of features in a non-privileged linear latent is not polysemanticity of neurons. The evidence is qualitative, with three seeds per condition, plots not rendered, and no uncertainty reported.

versions.untested_parts: Image classifiers and individual vision neurons.
Transformer language-model MLP neurons and token/context responses.
Tests sparse-feature superposition in toy models, not whether polysemantic neurons in trained networks generally arise from capacity pressure.
Polysemanticity arising from initialization, regularization, or training noise when there is enough capacity.
Activation-function, architecture, or regularization comparisons and their performance costs; alternative nonlinearities are proposed as future work only.
Whether apparent polysemanticity in trained networks resolves into a shared feature or related jobs with better tools.
How the measured prevalence of polysemanticity changes with activation range or explanation-scoring method.

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: Toy models with 20 input dimensions and 10 latent dimensions, including the conditional-importance setting
reader_labels.reason: The reported runs represent more features than latent dimensions, with interference, consistent with superposition in the tested toy setting (R1-R2). The fixed-importance and anti-correlated-feature comparisons also show superposition, with all 20 features represented in the latter (R3-R6).
